input:
The lifetime values that have been reported for the benchmark material by the two groups differ to a marked extent, and this disagreement is not readily explained by experimental scatter alone. A closer examination of the conditions under which the respective measurements were obtained suggests that the difference may be attributable, at least in part, to the test conditions that were employed. In one case the material was tested under conditions that departed in important respects from the conditions of the intended application, whereas in the other case the conditions were chosen so as to correspond more closely to those of the application in question.

On balance, and with the reservations that such a comparison necessarily entails, a limited preference is expressed for the values obtained under the conditions that match the intended service, although this preference is expressly conditional on that match holding for the application that the reader has in mind. Where the service conditions differ from both sets of test conditions, neither set of values can be adopted without further justification, and the disagreement between the two groups remains, for those cases, unresolved.
target:
For the benchmark material, the two groups report lifetime values that differ by more than either group's internal scatter. The difference follows the test conditions. One group tested under conditions removed from the intended service; the other tested under conditions matched to it, and the matched conditions are the ones whose values survive the comparison of methods. Scatter within a group's own runs measures the repeatability of that group's method. It does not measure the distance between two methods, and a difference that exceeds both scatters is a difference of method or of condition, not of chance.

The weighing therefore turns on condition. The group whose conditions match the intended service has run the test the application asks for; the other group has run a test whose relation to the application has to be argued, and the argument is not supplied in the report.

The preference is therefore limited and conditional. The values from the matched test conditions are preferred, and the condition on which the preference rests is the match itself: the service in view must be the service the test reproduced. Where the intended service departs from both sets of conditions, neither value carries over, and the disagreement stands for that case. The preference decides nothing about the material under conditions nobody has tested.
